title: Museum of Innocence
author: Orhan Pamuk
notes: This book made me reflect on my feelings and my understanding of love. Love can be something so fragile while also being something so powerful; love is for two, and at the same time, love can be kept alive only in one’s own mind. It describes so neatly how yearning changes one’s perception of the surroundings. It makes one deeply feel through words how innocent of a feeling love is. This novel forces you to read not only with eyes and brain, but with mind and heart.

title: Dom Casmurro
author: Machado de Assis
notes: Dom Casmurro is the memoir of a man who felt deeply in love to Capitu. He did everything that he could to finally marry her. Latter In life, he starts to think if his wife betrayed him or not with his best friend. This book has divided readers for more than one century into two groups based on this question: Did Capitu cheat? The author left us without answers, so depends on the reader to make its own opinions. This book invites you to see how love can change lives.

title: Chander and Sudha
author: Dharamvir Bharati
notes: The book explores what love is through the relationship between Sudha and Chander, and other characters that are part of their life. It shows the complexities of love, desire, morality, devotion and sacrifice. As the story progresses, it is fascinating to see how Sudha's and Chander's understanding of love changes. This makes them question whether idealizing love sometimes prevents us from accepting it in its natural, imperfect form. I would also recommend this book for its thoughtful exploration of marriage and its relationship with love. The story leaves us with uncomfortable realities of relationship, love, morality and how our own ideals shape the choices we make in the name of love.

title: The Threepenny Opera
author: Bertolt Brecht
notes: I chose Die Dreigroschenoper for the theme of laughter because Brecht uses laughter to wake the audience up, not to comfort it. We laugh at Peachum, who turns poverty into a business, and at Macheath, a bandit who behaves like a gentleman. But the Verfremdungseffekt (the “alienation effect”) keeps us from getting lost in the story: songs interrupt the action and characters speak to the audience, so we laugh, and then realise what we were laughing at. The ending, a last-second pardon that parodies the happy ending, makes that laughter bitter. I’d recommend it because it shows laughter as a way of seeing more clearly, and because “Mack the Knife” proves the point: a catchy tune about a murderer that we end up humming.

title: Waiting for Godot
author: Samuel Beckett
notes: Two men wait by a tree for someone called Godot, who never comes. It is funny, but not in the usual way. The humour is awkward and tragic, the kind of laugh that catches in your throat. Hats are swapped, trousers fall down, and every attempt to leave ends the same way: 'Let's go.' / They do not move. Vladimir and Estragon joke to fill the emptiness and keep each other going, and by the end you start to wonder what you are waiting for yourself. It is short, strange and surprisingly moving.

title: Before the Moon Forgets Us
author: Omar Khayyam
notes: I chose Omar Khayyam because he was much more than a poet: he was also a distinguished mathematician and astronomer, known for his work on cubic equations and his contribution to the Jalali calendar. What fascinates me is that, despite his remarkable achievements, his poetry never sounds as if he has solved the mystery of existence. He looks at the world with wonder and acknowledges how much remains unknowable. In this quatrain, the moon keeps shining while human life passes. I read Khayyam’s response to life’s uncertainty as an invitation to value the present without pretending we know what comes next.
